statement: Atmospheric trace species undergo photochemical and radical reactions whose rates depend on radiation, composition and conditions.
Stratospheric ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation, while ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant formed photochemically.
NOx and volatile organic compounds participate in networks that can produce photochemical smog and ozone under suitable conditions.
Aerosols affect atmospheric chemistry through composition, surfaces and optical interactions; Earth-system climate synthesis remains outside C10 ownership.
Water and soil chemistry depends on pH, acid-base equilibria, redox conditions and dissolved or sorbed species.
Chemical speciation influences mobility, bioavailability and analytical measurement of elements and contaminants.
Sorption to minerals and organic matter can retard contaminant transport without necessarily destroying the contaminant.
Sampling and analysis must distinguish dissolved, particulate and operationally defined fractions when interpreting environmental concentrations.
Pollutant fate depends on sources, transport, partitioning, chemical transformation and removal processes.
Hazard describes inherent potential for harm, whereas risk also depends on exposure or dose and context.
Persistence and bioaccumulation can increase concern for some contaminants but do not alone determine health outcome.
Environmental toxicant chemistry characterizes identity, transformation and exposure media; health synthesis belongs to X03 boundary.
Industrial chemical processes combine reaction, separation, heat/mass transfer and recycle operations to transform feedstocks into products.
Conversion, yield and selectivity are distinct process metrics.
Recycle can improve raw-material utilization but may accumulate impurities or increase separation and energy demands.
Process evaluation includes safety, waste, emissions and energy/material use in addition to throughput.
Catalysts change kinetic pathways and rates without changing the overall equilibrium constant at fixed temperature.
Industrial catalyst performance requires activity, selectivity and stability, not activity alone.
Heterogeneous catalysis involves transport, adsorption, surface reaction and desorption steps whose relative rates can control performance.
Catalyst deactivation can arise from poisoning, fouling, sintering or chemical transformation.
Green chemistry seeks to design chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substance use and generation where practicable.
Waste prevention is generally preferable to treating or cleaning waste after formation.
Solvent, reagent, energy, hazard and feedstock choices create trade-offs; no single green metric captures every environmental consequence.
Natural, renewable or biodegradable does not automatically mean chemically safe.
Atom economy measures the fraction of reactant atoms incorporated into the desired product according to reaction stoichiometry.
Atom economy differs from percent yield: a high-yield reaction can still generate stoichiometric by-products.
Atom economy does not include solvent, catalyst loading, energy, toxicity or downstream separation impacts.
Reaction and process metrics should be combined when comparing alternatives rather than optimizing one metric alone.
A material life cycle can include raw-material extraction, production, use, reuse or recovery, recycling and end-of-life treatment.
Life-cycle comparisons depend on functional unit and system boundary; changing either can change conclusions.
Recycling can reduce virgin-material demand but requires collection, separation, processing and quality retention; it is not impact-free.
Chemical/material lifecycle reasoning can identify burden shifting across stages, while Earth-system, health, food and policy synthesis remain secondary boundaries.
